One of the greatest RPG games I've ever played, and I say that with 100% truth. Even with this game being over a decade old, it still holds up. If you haven't played and Persona games before and you like Turn Based RPG's, you won't regret this game. If you're tired of hanging out with friends or fishing, you can enter the TV and start fighting Shadows and leveling up your Personas and friends. Many of the strongest Persona are unlocked once you increase your social levels higher. Time: 60+ Hours IF you play through the whole game, get the true ending (yes there a true ending), and get the Golden final dungeon (which is seperate, yet together with the true ending), the game is over 60 hours. Persona 4 Golden A Journey Worth Remembering Rating: 8/10 Some games entertain you, some challenge you, and others leave behind a lingering sense of nostalgia when the journey finally comes to an end. Persona 4 Golden manages to accomplish all three, delivering an experience that, despite its occasional frustrations, became something genuinely difficult to leave behind. Set in the quiet, seemingly unremarkable town of Inaba, Persona 4 Golden gradually transforms an ordinary year into an unforgettable journey of mystery, friendship, self-discovery, and the pursuit of truth. What begins as an investigation into a series of disturbing murders evolves into something far more personal: a story about confronting the parts of ourselves we would rather conceal, accepting the people we are, and recognizing the importance of the connections we forge along the way. At its heart, Persona 4 Golden is a celebration of human connection. Its characters are not merely companions accompanying the protagonist through another supernatural adventure; they are individuals with their own insecurities, ambitions, contradictions, and struggles. Their relationships give Inaba its warmth, transforming what might otherwise be an ordinary setting into a place that feels remarkably alive. As the days pass and friendships deepen, the thought of eventually leaving this little town becomes increasingly bittersweet. Among the cast, Chie Satonaka stands out as my personal favorite. Her energetic personality, straightforward attitude, and enthusiasm for martial arts make her an immediately memorable presence. Beneath her humor and confidence, however, lies a character whose desire to protect others gives her personality greater depth. She embodies much of what makes the Investigation Team so endearing: the ability to laugh together, support one another, and remain imperfectly, unapologetically human. Of course, the journey is not without its shortcomings. The pacing can occasionally feel uneven, and the combat encounters sometimes cross the line between challenging and exhausting. Certain battles demand considerable patience, turning what should be an exciting test of strategy into a prolonged war of attrition. Ameno-sagiri was a particularly memorable example, requiring approximately twenty attempts before finally falling. Even Izanami, who proved somewhat easier, demanded another ten attempts. These encounters tested my patience, but overcoming them ultimately made the victories feel earned. Hollow Forest deserves particular mention. Its unusual mechanics, especially its punishing approach to SP management, force the player to reconsider familiar strategies. It can be frustrating, but it also distinguishes itself from the game's other dungeons. Surviving its challenges and ultimately defeating Kusumi-no-Okami made reaching the final stretch of the journey feel all the more satisfying. Yet the greatest strength of Persona 4 Golden lies not in its combat, mysteries, or supernatural spectacle, but in the emotional significance of its conclusion. After spending an entire year alongside these characters, the prospect of leaving Inaba carries a weight that is difficult to articulate. The farewell scenes capture the bittersweet nature of growing up and moving forward: friendships can endure even when circumstances change, and meaningful experiences do not lose their value simply because they have ended. The Golden epilogue provides a particularly welcome sense of closure. Seeing Yu return to Inaba and reunite with his friends is a beautiful reminder of the bonds established throughout the story. It is not merely a celebration of having solved the mystery; it is a celebration of the people who made the journey worthwhile. The reunion offers a comforting answer to the sadness of departure, suggesting that while a chapter may close, the relationships formed within it need not disappear. Despite these strengths, Persona 4 Golden does not surpass Persona 3 in my personal ranking. Persona 3's atmosphere, themes, and emotional impact remain more compelling to me. Nevertheless, comparing the two does not diminish what Persona 4 accomplishes. Where Persona 3 leaves a profound impression through its contemplation of mortality and the meaning of life, Persona 4 finds much of its beauty in the warmth of companionship, the courage to seek truth, and the simple happiness of belonging somewhere. Ultimately, Persona 4 Golden is an experience whose imperfections are difficult to ignore, but whose emotional strengths are equally difficult to forget. Its most memorable achievement is making Inaba feel like somewhere worth returning to—not because its streets are extraordinary, but because of the people who inhabit them. And perhaps that is the most fitting way to describe the feeling of watching its credits roll: not disappointment that the story has ended, but gratitude for having experienced it at all. Final Rating: 8/10 A heartfelt odyssey through mystery, friendship, and the search for truth—a reminder that even the most ordinary places can become extraordinary when shared with the right people.

During my time in Inaba, I found pieces of myself scattered across nearly all of its residents. Persona 4 Golden hit me in a way I didn't see coming, quietly forcing me to reflect on my own flaws, fears, and the exact moments I tried to hide from who I really was. Across so many different lives, I saw my own struggles laid bare, Ai shielding her vulnerability behind a cruel facade, Yukiko aching to escape a path she felt trapped in, Yumi drowning in grief and resentment over an absent parent, and Kou suffocating under the weight of an identity he never chose for himself. I watched Kanji fight the shame of not fitting in, Yosuke mask a deep, haunting loneliness with humor, Hisano carry the devastating guilt of her past, and Shu crumble under forced perfection. As I grew older, I realized that at a very important time in my life, I truly related to these characters. I saw myself in their triumphs and their worst moments, and their significance wasn't just in the stories they told, but in what they taught me. They gave me the courage, quite literally, to face myself, especially the parts of myself I didn't like, and showed me that accepting those flaws is the only way we ever truly learn to stop running. I think that's what makes Persona 4 so special to me. Its message isn't that we can overcome every flaw, erase every regret, or become the people we wish we were overnight. It's that we have to be honest with ourselves before we can ever hope to change. There's something deeply uncomfortable about that. It's so much easier to construct an image of ourselves that we can live with, to bury the things we're ashamed of, or to pretend that the parts of us we dislike belong to someone else. But those parts don't simply disappear because we refuse to acknowledge them. If anything, they gain more control over us the longer we spend running away. Watching these characters confront themselves helped me understand that being flawed doesn't make you undeserving of love, and that acknowledging the worst parts of yourself doesn't mean reducing yourself to them. You can be lonely and still be loved. You can be afraid of who you are and still find the courage to accept yourself. You can make mistakes, hurt people, and carry regrets without allowing those things to define the rest of your life. None of that makes the process easy, but I think that's the point. Accepting yourself isn't a single moment of realization after which everything suddenly makes sense. It's something you have to keep choosing, even when it's uncomfortable. Looking back, I don't think Persona 4 simply helped me understand its characters. It helped me understand myself. In a strange way, spending time with these fictional people gave me the space to confront things about my own life that I might not have known how to put into words otherwise. Their struggles made me feel less alone, and their growth reminded me that understanding yourself is not always a pleasant experience, but it's a necessary one. Sometimes, the people who help us grow the most are the ones who make us realize just how much growing we still have to do. I'll always carry a piece of Inaba with me. Not because it gave me all the answers, but because it taught me to stop being so afraid of the questions. It also taught me to appreciate the people who come into my life, to look beyond the surface and understand that everyone is fighting battles I may never fully understand. Much like the people I met in Inaba, my friends and the people I've met throughout my life have helped me understand myself in ways I never could have on my own. And if there's one thing I'll always take away from Persona 4, it's that learning to accept yourself is important, but so is finding people who make you feel like you don't have to hide who you are in the first place. In the end, I think that's what makes Persona 4 mean so much to me. It reminded me that accepting ourselves is rarely something we accomplish alone, and that the people who come into our lives can change us in ways we don't fully understand until years later. I'm grateful that, at a time when I needed it, this game helped me see that in myself and in the people around me.

I’m coming into Persona 3 Reload as someone who never touched the original or the PSP version. My entry point to the series was Persona 5 Royal, and honestly, Reload is one of the best things that could’ve happened to newcomers like me. You don’t need any prior history with the franchise to get completely swept away by this game. What really hit me is how much heart this game has. The story, the characters, the music, the sense that your time with the SEES crew is slipping away day by day. It all builds into something that genuinely sticks with you. I got attached to this cast in a way I didn’t expect, and by the time the credits rolled, I felt hollow. Not because the game ended badly, but because it made me care so much that saying goodbye hurt. Very few games have done that to me. I’ve noticed a lot of longtime fans are weighed down by nostalgia, especially those who played the original or FES/Portable. I get it, those versions mean a lot to people. But as someone with no baggage, I can say that Reload stands on its own as a fantastic experience. And speaking of the female protagonist, I can’t help but wonder how much more special this would’ve been with her route included. Even without ever playing the older versions, I’m curious how that would’ve played out here. It would’ve made an already great game even better. If you’re coming from Persona 5 and wondering whether to jump into 3, don’t hesitate. Play it. Just be ready for the emptiness afterward. Rating: 9/10

I was constantly [i]forcing[/i] myself to continue playing this game, out of sheer stubbornness, for the promise of "it gets better". Imagine a friend shows up and tells you about this awesome TV series. It goes like this "so it has 8 seasons, but the first 5 or 6 are kinda boring, nothing substancial happens and nothing about the plot will make any sense, but it gets better later I promise!". That is Persona 3. Calling it a "slow burn" is atrocious. And look, I've been playing JRPGs for two decades, I was not expecting a game based on a high-school setting with literal teenagers as protagonists to reinvent the wheel or be the absolute peak of storytelling. But you gotta give me something, man. Holding the plot hostage for ~40 hours is not it. Even when things actually started to move forward, the "plot twists" were not that interesting to justify the pacing. The "antagonists" did absolutely nothing for me... (and don't even get me started on the Chidori thing). I could probably have still finished it, or even given it a positive review, if the gameplay part was interesting enough. However, after 40ish hours of only having very few places to visit for the social part, and going through [b]hundreds[/b] of floors of the [b]same dungeon[/b], with the [b]exact same enemies[/b] with a different color tint or background every now and then, I lost interest in the gameplay part. Running through randomly generated floors gets old really fast when there's nothing to keep things fresh or at least break up the monotony. Even playing the game on hard from the start didn't require any kind of strategy or added any variety, as the only thing it does is turning enemies into health sponges to stretch playtime. Dropped it down to story mode at around floor 170 and started skipping days until I decided to just watch the endings on youtube instead. Oh, and if you want the 100% full story experience and closure, you'll need the overpriced premmium edition/expansion pass to play the epilogue DLC (no, it's not in the deluxe edition)... While it is not [i]mandatory[/i], it sucks that it is not included in the base game, because it was cut to be sold apart for $$$ reasons. Watch it on youtube instead to save money and time. Unless you, for some reason, absolutely loved the idea of grinding the same dungeon over and over again and wanted even more of it. [hr] Overall, that's a sad no from me. I liked the main characters and the overall more mature setting, cringe moments notwhitstanding. There are some genuine good moments and messages here; sadly, those are very few and far between, buried amongst several hours of repetitive gameplay and glacial story pacing. On the good side: the music and the animations are top notch. Can't argue about that.

I tried playing this through to the end, but realized by the time I reached January in game that I was just playing to 'complete' it as if it had become a chore - and I dropped the game flat out. I came from really enjoying the weird and dark vibes of SMT V:V, and then enjoying the linear but engaging character development and adventure in Metaphor: ReFantazio only to jump into this game and really struggle to connect with any of the characters, let alone the sheer amount of fluff that slows this game down to a grinding halt. I had almost stopped playing around Summer time with the same gripes with my experience before reading how things really 'ramp up' closer to the end of the year.. That resulted in a push to get there and see what I was missing out on... only to experience a couple of story progressing moments and a plot twist that just didn't outweigh the amount of grind it took to get there. It's got a clean graphical style, good quality voice acting, and smooth bug-free gameplay but all of that good is heavily diluted by how much uninteresting dialogue there is with side characters that I just didn't care about. The story could be so much shorter, maybe that's a sign of how my tastes have changed since games like this were making marks in 2006. The tower is very repetitive, and in order to progress at a high level towards the end game you have to grind a ton to afford leveling up your persona team/filling out the compendium. Then it was back to school and running around the small sandbox trying to find a reason to care and think about some of the persona social link stories. Off the cuff I'd say this story and game being condensed into say 20 hours would really change things. I think it's a consequence of being such an old game and they could have really benefitted from a remake rather than just a remaster for the graphics and audio (though I didn't play the original so maybe there was more done). Make social link stories more optional, 3-5 levels instead of 9 each, add something interesting to the tower phase that ties into the story....add a mute button to some of the repetitive chatter you end up hearing 1,200 times from each party member. Add a skip animation button for AOA's and Persona Abilities or shorten the animations after the 1st time or something. Reduce the insane amount of prompts requiring click throughs just to hear dialogue that doesn't mean anything. Game looks like it's currently 70% off and even then I'd say the story could have been an email and you should really ask yourself if you have 100 hours to burn for the sake of it. I'd steer you towards the earlier mentioned Shin Megami Tensei 5 or Metaphor ReFantazio for better titles by ATLUS... Or look into the latest Persona 6 which I do have my now-wary eye on.. I'd probably rate it a 5/10, but I can say it had potential to be reworked into a really solid 8-9/10.

The plot itself is good, the music is great, the game itself looks and sounds amazing. The characters are fun despite that nothing you do actually affects them. Weirdly enough, despite that this game was released on pc, it's borderline unplayable on keyboard and mouse without mods, which is strange because persona 5 works just fine. Even controller sense is completely jacked and I had to download mods to fix it. Social links are a joke, probably one of my biggest gripes with persona games even if 5 did them better. They have little to no interaction, as almost nothing you say means or affects anything, and are little more than just a npc telling you their mini-story while you watch how events play out. Oh, and once you're done with the social link? Well don't expect to see them ever again because there's nothing left to do with them. Including characters you've romanced as well. Great part is that all you get for doing them is more xp on personas of that social links particular arcana, and a bonus persona that you'd never know how to make unless you looked it up. Majority of the social link characters are enjoyable but gameplay wise it's a seriously lacking mechanic for something core to the game. Perhaps it can be called a skill issue but I have almost never had an enjoyable experience with boss fights in this game. The vast majority of the bosses can be beaten with nothing more than simply grinding it out with very little effort or brain. The only bosses I ever did struggle with were almost purely because of aliment spam, which was able to be worked around but very, very annoying. Even worse, the vast majority of the game is boss fights, as there is almost no occasion where fighting ads is actually necessary or practical for progression. Once you've completed the two social links available at nighttime and your social stats just as I did about three quarters into the game, you'll realize very quickly that there is literally nothing you can do at night apart from going to Tartarus to grind (even though you've likely already gotten to your border floor) along with some minor things like making 4000ish yen (half of one fight in Tartarus) or increasing one of you're persona's stats by 3 even though that persona will likely just get thrown out anyway for a higher level one. Half of a day being completely useless took a lot of the fun out of the game for me as it usually ended up with multiple days of doing a social link during the day and sleep in evening. Persona 3 isn't a bad game by any means, but it's also not a good game. It's a game with outstanding art and music, a good enough plot, memorable characters, and a fitting combat system. That alone is enough for some, but to me this game is also majorly flawed in some parts that make the game's over 50 hour run time a major slog to get through. It's not a game I would've come remotely close to finishing had I not played other persona's before it, and certainly not something I'd recommend to most people before 5 or 4.

I have complicated feelings on it, but ultimately I didn't like it. The main issue is how it handles it's subject matter. Japan has a strange relationship with suicide, out of just over 200 countries listed, some sources like CountryCassette have Japan as #8 in the world for suicide rates, that's above Ukraine and two before Russia who are literally at war; and US is listed at #30. Why Japan has this issue is never going to be perfectly clear, but it's tolerant views on suicide do cause concern. For example, people can be brought up to think that it's more "honourable", be it to their family, their family's ghosts, or just to some vague collective abstraction of a unified societal value; that it's better to stop existing anymore over normal things like losing your job, or even simply leaving it due to imbalanced work:life ratio; it's a despicable, cruel and cultural capitalistic distortion and mockery of any substantive meaning of life, and this is just one example. The game to it's credit does at least TRY to speak on this. You will talk to NPCs and team members going through all sorts of issues, including those like losing or hating their jobs, and they don't have a magical fix. At the time this game was written, there was a push in government to understand and decrease this death rate; the game does, through it's apathy syndrome context, impart somewhat what it must feel like to be aware of what seems like a shadow looming over everyone. My biggest issue then is here: the main character; you. You see, another contributing factor posited to the way suicide is seen in Japan, is said to be that your self worth matters less than your worth through the fickle and unreliable eyes of others, hence tying back to shame and "dishonour" if you fall short. The main character absolutely does nothing but further feed this fallacy; it's entirely tone-deaf. Your character is the most attractive, the most important, the most talented, the coolest and the most charming person in existence and it's all completely effortless; all he does is walk around nodding his head and everyone either loves him, admires him or is in envy of him. You make deep, meaningful and permanent connections by looking at people, blank-faced with your hands in your pockets, responding with simple, single-sentence empty platitudes, and of course by nodding, you even nod over the phone sometimes. On one hand the game themes it's entire story as an attempt to address a truly dire reality affecting millions, yet on the other hand has you play as a character who is not just without faults, but has an unnatural ability to succeed at anything. He has absolutely no bad traits, and is able to navigate anything from simple social appearances to world-ending issues with complete composure, even as his team falls apart around him, until he talks to them of course. What kind of message is this, especially to the young? Just do a bit and it will work out? Or all you have to do is stare at people with your hands in your pockets, nod a lot and say "there there" and they'll be your best friend or faun over you? I just felt there was so much substance completely undermined by this, I just could not take it seriously. Further, the comments and disclaimers made it seem like this game would be crushingly deep, but because of your infallibility, the only depth possible is from your imperfect team. That said, the extent of their arc is that something will happen, they say they want to die a few times, then either you or other team mates help them feel better; the game is most effective when the team members, the actually troubled people, help each other out, because their experiences have more substance. Some of these conclusion scenes are meaningful and well written, a couple are incredibly vapid. Overall, mainly because of the main character, the deeper meaning of this game is fundamentally warped in my opinion; and completely backwards sometimes. Not everyone will see it this way, clearly, and even if they did, they may still get genuine comfort simply from the fact the game is interacting, in some way, with real issues. I've read comments often on how Kurt Cobain saved people's lives, and as someone who likes him and his music, I can say it's not clear to me why, but I did also find comfort in listening to his music during depression, despite his ending; so it's not always logical how art inspires the better feelings in us. Our conflicting experiences are valid. With the main character aside, I did have similar issues with some of the team: Junpei is insufferable; he's an egotistical, obnoxious, petulant and desperate pervert. Other than him taking the time out to introduce himself to you, and apologising if he messed up, he has very few redeeming qualities. It's ironic then that dealing with him is a better idea of what life is really like; sometimes you have to put up with people who are insufferable, and it's not always what to do or if it's fixable. The most interesting member. Takeba I found less annoying, but not entirely; as much as I dislike Junpei, when Takeba interacts with him, every single word out of her mouth is criticism or shot at him; she is constantly putting him down. She even finds someone talking about bullying another student, and responds "I hate people like that" and I could feel my "YOU'RE LIKE THAT" building up strongly; you can see why I would have issues taking the game seriously on how it addresses bullying too. If I find someone I don't like, I don't interact with them, I find no joy in tearing them down, Takeba does. That aside, that's her biggest fault, otherwise she just doesn't have much personality, I can't really describe how she is. She's generally kind and good, to you of course, because everyone loves you. As alluded to, she is a character who has one of the better scenes though, where she takes the time to confront another troubled team member. Ken turned out to be the character I liked the least; he's a manipulative, scheming murderous little bastard and the way the game resolves this is almost entirely devoid of depth. After this became apparent, I refused to interact with him again for the entire game, other than when it was forced. Finally, Koromaru. A cute dog is hard to be annoyed at, but unfortunately, he's voiced by a human pretending to be a dog, and you might not have the same experience here, but hearing someone, even voice actors as great as these, moake loud, shrill fake whimpers and barks directly into my ear was unbearable, and during fights especially he does not be quiet for a second, so like Ken, I couldn't stand his company, but for different reasons. I do appreciate the other members a bit more, but the biggest compliment I can make is they're not annoying or bad people, I still can't quite describe them. The biggest laughs came from an Aigis quote, and non-team member Elizabeth. Elizabeth was an absolute joy to hang-out with frankly. Additionally, I'm a big RWBY fan, and I have a feeling Aigis and Mitsuru inspired Penny and Weiss, which was cool to see. Lastly, the actual gameplay. I admit I am not used to JRPGs, and the reason I wanted to play this game was to start as early as feasible on one of it's most acclaimed franchises. I did have a lot of issues, such as your team saying the same thing over and OVER again, and I'm quite sensitive to obnoxious audio anyway, as established with Koromaru, but even with their endless yapping I was eventually able to zone it out, and further in the game entered a flow-state where I couldn't even hear them. It took over 60 hours, however, and I didn't get into the flow state often. Overall, it's okay to play mostly. The positives: Elizabeth, some sweet side stories, the persona mechanics, some of the levels in Tartarus are gorgeous. The systems are deep too, lots to update and work towards and do. Just sadly, I didn't enjoy this otherwise. I can't recommend it.

I wasn't expecting for another Atlus game to compete one-to-one against a landmark such as Persona 5, however, I'm glad for that statement to be debunked by my experience with Persona 3 Reload. It is true that the game has a fair amount of flaws (mostly the main dungeon being a huge hallway with some randomizer aspects that spice it a bit), but I consider most of them to be a part of the era when the game was originally released. Story-wise the game is precisely what you would expect from an 100+ hours jRPG, a roller-coaster of emotions and well written-characters with some goofiness in between, but where the game excels over Persona 5 is in how it depicts the struggle of our "anime-friendos", in a way that feels way more personal and grounded than that of the grandiose and flamboyant depiction of heroism presented by P5. This is a game that doesn't try anything you may have not seen before, the battles are based on the same SMT inspired system we are all so familiar with at this point, yet it's perfectly accompanied by Soejima's aesthetic, Azumi Takahashi's soundtrack and a leitmotif that goes a little beyond the "friends we make along the way" cliché. Definitely try it if you are up for that!

Ok, simply put this game is very solid. Putting it bluntly, it is worth your money and is a good 7.5-8/10. I will not give examples from the story to avoid spoilers and keep the experience as pure as possible. Starting off with performance, it was very strong. I kept a stable 120 fps without any drops. I didn't have any performance issues so that should not be a deal breaker Now, moving onto the actual game, there are some clear problems that this game has but I would argue that the pros indeed outweigh the cons. The story in this game is alright. It is likely not going to blow you away if I explain the story (I wont due to spoilers) but what makes this game truly special is the outstanding narration. The way the story is told, with the many subtle metaphors sprinkled through and the characters you develop relations with, make this game truly great. I wouldn't be lying when I say the devil is in the details. In fact, I would argue that this is some of the best use of metaphors and storytelling I've seen in a video game. (Story is NOT equal to storytelling) On the note of the story, the story does have somewhat a moral binary in terms of what you can do as the mc. I would have liked a tad bit more nuance but it makes sense for this type of game to have the structure it does. On top of the moral binary in some instances, the dialogue is sometimes a bit too on the nose and too direct. That isn't a big problem by any means in terms of how the story unfolds and how its told but instead it comes across as a bit clunky. It isn't something to break deals over, but its just something I have noticed and would like to point out. Next, this game does pull the power of friendship card towards the end, but it doesn't come across as cliche. At first I thought it was a waste of an ending, but the whole story built up to that moment, and form what I have watched in the DLC (I do not own it, but friends do and so I was able to experience it) The reasoning for the power of friendship changes from cliche to more so a desperate, final stand. the more I thought about it, the more I enjoyed it The power of friend ship unlike other games to force a happy ending, is done to drive home the core narrative of the game, which is up for you to figure out. I am very happy this game isn't afraid to pull any punches. Now this is indeed a persona game, so you will have a cast of characters. Now the main issue is the main cast actually feels slightly more shallow that the side characters (which I will get to). They do go through emotional turmoil, they have very deep and changing moments in the story, event with an overarching personality type. Each character has a unique aspect to the table and their struggles reflect that they show their growth and many sides to their character. However, I wanted more of that. I felt a couple specific characters had SO MUCH more room for growth and potential for the story. Through the story, there are many events that happen (spoilers) and through the story the characters drop certain lines. The story however, never addresses those and characters resolution with conflicts come to a close a bit too quickly. I would have liked a longer time for that. That brings me to the next issue with the gameplay loop (tying to the previous point). Now I do enjoy exploring the primary dungeon in this game and building socials is always great, however there are massive blocks of time in which nearly nothing happens. While your actually exploring the dungeon, the encounters are fun to fight and the moment to moment game ranges from relaxing to strategical (mostly depends on what your doing. ). Grinding the tower does get tedious after some time, but that's mostly during the middle of the game during its slowest point. The difficulty can be shifted as you wish so I will not say much, but the harder difficulties are for sure hard and require you to prepare ahead of time. Tying the gameplay with the characters, in the middle of the game you mostly play for the sake of playing and just try to progress to the next objective. Simply put, there is a lot of downtime in the middle of the game in which there is simply nothing to do and you just need to push forward. The game is really at its peak during the latter quarter of it, which is a shame since most of the character development and story happens, which is quite a shame in my opinion. I wish the game moved faster in the middle then slowed down nearing the end. The game spent too much time in some areas and not enough time in others. I love that its a slow burn but sometimes its as if the flame hasn't even started. Moving onto the side characters, there are a couple which although were fleshed out and had multiple sides to them, they are not likeable. I know that might be the point for those characters but that doesn't change my view on them. However, that is 2-3 characters. Every other character is very deep and fleshed out. They come with their own backstory and can change across the relationship. They aren't stagnant and have one emotion or type of character. Instead its used to represent an arch type. If you are on the fence of getting this game or not, I would highly recommend that you get this game. The message that it tries to convey, the way it goes about giving you that story is actually amazing. Don't go into this game expecting a quick play and done game, it takes a while. I am glad I bought this game and you should as well. (as for the DLC, I would personally not get it, i would say you would have a much more fun experience watching the cutscenes or hearing elsewhere.)

For starters, wow. Never in my entire life has the ending of a video game made me cry. When I picked this up I thought I was just satisfying my crave for turn based RPG's and while it did do that, it also turned into 66 hours (thats what my ingame save file says) of the most emotionally moving gameplay. Persona 3 Reload truly embodies the ideas of Momento Mori, "remember you will die one day". Every decision you make in this game has impact towards the ending as your constantly reminded that your choices do matter. THE GAMEPLAY WAS SO ENCAPSULATING. I did not think at all that this game would be so slice of life and action packed at the same time. It felt a lot like how spiderman as a character works; Lives 2 lives, tries his best in both and then they eventually collide. You'd go from boosting your social skills, making new connections with genuinely the most interesting cast of characters (AKIHIKO MY GOAT) and i'm not kidding using the power of friendship to help you beat up monsters using Jojo stands. Sick ass idea. WHATS BETTER? THE MUSIC OF COURSE. Do you know what Acid-Jazz is? I DO NOW AND ITS GREAT. SPOILER WARNING: This review contains spoiler-free sections about the gameplay social links soundtrack and UI as well as a marked spoiler section detailing the story character reactions the ending and the Episode Aegis DLC. A Masterpiece of Atmosphere UI and Human Depth: My Entry Point Persona 3 Reload was my very first Persona game ever and my first step into this franchise. Some people often complain that you should not start with Reload because Tartarus is so exhausting and hard to endure (which is totally understandable it was a real pain!). But even with that grind the game was simply peak from start to finish. The characters the world the music and absolutely everything was peak. Persona 3 Reload is a dark profound masterpiece that bluntly asks you the question: What does it actually mean that our time on Earth is finite? The entire game relentlessly revolves around the theme of death the acceptance of the inevitable and this gloomy melancholic feeling that lingers throughout your entire playthrough. The Soundtrack: Absolute Peak Shoji Meguros overhauled soundtrack reimagined with the vocals of Lotus Juice and Azumi Takahashi is pure magic. Every track hits the spot: Iwatodai Dorm: The absolute highlight for dorm life! When you chill in the dorm in the evening and listen to this extremely relaxed song with its smooth hip hop beats in the background it is pure comfort. A track you would love to play at home just to chill! Color Your Night: The perfect relaxed vibe for nightlife and exploring the city. Mass Destruction: The iconic battle theme featuring Lotus Juices vocals that still gets you hyped even after dozens of fights. Burn My Dread and Its Going Down Now: Deliver incredible intensity during major fights and ambushes. Memories of You Kimi no Kioku: A gorgeous yet emotionally destructive song in the finale. When you hear this track you get almost something like PTSD from deep seated pain and it triggers that exact crushing painful feeling like at Cyberpunk Edgerunners. Pure uncut sadness. Gameplay Criticism: The Repetitive Climb of Tartarus As great as the story and combat are Tartarus is without a doubt the weakest part of the game: Extreme Repetition: Fighting your way through over 200 floors of Tartarus feels extremely tedious. You see the exact same hallway designs and floor patterns easily 30 times in a row. Artificial Story Gates: Having the path upwards regularly blocked off and forcing you to wait a full month for the next story segment stretches out the dungeon crawling unnecessarily. Tough Encounters: Since you cannot quickly and easily dispatch weaker Shadows without jumping through extra hoops the monthly climb feels like a long grueling grind. The Characters Yukari Sanada and Aigis Authentic Depth and Yukari: What makes the characters feel so genuinely real is their authentic fear of death. Yukari definitely one of my favorite characters shows through her panic at the beginning that she is no invincible machine but a completely normal vulnerable girl who is terrified of that gun. She grows on you immensely over the course of the game and is simply a sweetheart. Sanada as the Big Brother: Akihiko Sanada feels like a true big brother who looks out for you. As a dedicated and hardcore boxer he is a massive pillar of strength and cares deeply for the group. Aigis and her Humanity: Even though Aigis is technically a robot she gradually becomes more and more human throughout the journey and shows genuine deep care for the protagonist. Junpei as the Best Bro: Junpei starts out as this typical sometimes clueless goofball friend but in such a funny and lovable way that you just have to take him into your heart. The Romance: I chose Yukari for the romance and took her completely to heart. Even though you often hear that she comes across as much harsher in older versions like Portable in Reload she is simply a sweet girl who gets incredibly close to you. The Aegis DLC Episode Aegis The Aegis DLC Episode Aegis is a cool addition but brings mixed feelings. The fights at the end especially those exhausting annoying double battles against your own teammates often felt like a frustrating grind especially since I bulldozed through with DLC Personas out of time constraints. Still the narrative character depth where you learn even more about the painful past of your teammates is totally worthwhile. And it simply breaks your heart when you realize in the DLC how badly Yukari who could not care less what the others think or whether the sacrifice was supposedly necessary just damn well wants the protagonist back! SPOILER SECTION Story Conflicts Characters and Finale ACHTUNG SPOILER! Please only read this if you have already finished the game or do not care about story details. The brilliant and tragic twist is that Aigis herself is directly responsible for this: During that fateful tragedy years ago where the parents of the protagonist died Aigis fought against Death and sealed the entity Pharos or rather Ryoji directly inside the young protagonist to prevent Nyx from coming. Because of this deep connection Aigis instinctively has a strong sense of foreboding and suspicion towards Ryōji long before anyone else realizes who he truly is because deep down she senses what he means and what danger he brings. Junpei Chidori and the Human Conflict in the Team: What makes S.E.E.S so special is that the group does not react like sanitized video game heroes but like real deeply terrified teenagers. A huge highlight is Junpei and his dynamic with Chidori: When you think Junpei is going to die that day Chidori sacrifices her own life to protect him from death which is an absolutely epic and heartbreaking scene. At the same time this makes Junpei so extremely authentic: When it comes to light that the protagonist unknowingly entered into this contract with death during his very first awakening and thereby rang the bells of death because Ryōji and Pharos were awakened by the awakening of the powers sheer despair breaks out. Junpei completely loses his temper and screams at his best friend asking why he did not simply die back then in front of that Shadow. This shows pure raw humanity and the fear of death. When a person realizes how close death is and that their own best friend was unknowingly the foundation for this catastrophe reacting out of sheer self-preservation and deep despair is brutally honest. Ryōji Mochizuki and the Truth about Nyx: The revelation that Ryōji with whom you previously spent totally normal time is actually the Avatar of Nyx and the harbinger of doom is a massive plot twist that pushes the team to their moral and emotional limits. The Ending the Emotional Breakdown and the Menu Aftermath: The finale is hard to top in terms of emotional weight. After the victory over Nyx comes the time-skip to Graduation Day. Everyone is sitting downstairs in the auditorium when a spark suddenly jumps to the team members while memories of the Dark Hour initially seemed wiped out. They remember the promise they made to meet up on the school roof after the fight. In the final minutes everyone sprints upstairs. You chat casually with Aigis while the eyelids of the protagonist grow heavier and heavier. The formal option to close your eyes changes nothing about the inevitable reality: As a character you die because you used up all your life force for the Great Seal to protect everyone. When I was on a Discord call with a buddy late at night in the summer I muted myself briefly because I sobbed all the way through the credits. With tears in my eyes I had to tell my friend afterwards that the ending was wonderful but I needed a quick break.

GAMEPLAY Persona 5 Royal features a turn-based JRPG combat system built around exploiting enemy weaknesses, knocking them down, and capitalizing on those openings. While the game offers numerous elemental affinities, most function identically outside of specific Technical attack interactions. What initially feels like a deep combat system quickly reveals itself to be shallow. Progression is equally disappointing. Combat becomes repetitive within the first 10 hours, with little mechanical evolution to keep encounters interesting. The game even provides abilities like Insta-kill, allowing players to bypass ordinary encounters entirely. It's almost an acknowledgment of how tedious its combat eventually becomes. STORY The story begins with a compelling premise: a teenager wronged by society, navigating a deeply unjust world. The opening establishes intriguing characters and a promising narrative centered around rebellion and societal corruption. Unfortunately, the writing loses momentum roughly a third of the way through. The narrative becomes predictable, character development feels repetitive, and the social commentary gradually loses its impact. The greatest weakness is the lack of restraint. Conversations reiterate information the player already knows, story arcs drag beyond their natural conclusions, and the pacing suffers under excessive dialogue. By the time I reached the additional Royal content, I had lost the motivation to continue. Between the mundane gameplay, mediocre writing, and overwhelming bloat, another lengthy chapter felt exhausting rather than exciting. PRESENTATION If there's one area where Persona 5 Royal excels, it's presentation. The soundtrack is groovy, catchy, and memorable. The interface oozes personality, with striking typography, fluid animations, and an unmistakable visual identity. Unfortunately, this extraordinary presentation often feels like a beautiful facade concealing a far less interesting experience. The underlying gameplay and narrative simply lack comparable depth. FINAL THOUGHTS Of my roughly 90 hours with Persona 5 Royal, I genuinely enjoyed perhaps the first 25. Beyond that point, the experience became increasingly predictable, mundane, and one-dimensional. The problem isn't necessarily that its individual systems are terrible. It's that there isn't enough mechanical or narrative variety to sustain such an enormous adventure. Persona 5 Royal looks and sounds phenomenal, but too often mistakes length for depth, repetition for substance, and style for meaningful progression. An extraordinary sense of style. I only wish the game beneath it had been equally extraordinary.

[h1]What Psych Students Think Their Degree Does[/h1] [h2]Its retardedly good[/h2] I’ve been on a binge of JRPGs lately and I happen to FINALLY finish persona 5. It only took close to 10 years. Persona’s what happens when you give psych students, steeped in the forbidden knowledge of the occult, too much money to make an anime pseudo dating game. Turns out, that shit slaps. Also works pretty well on the steamdeck so no excuse to play this on the fly. Like most people I enjoyed Persona on the playstation when it first came out. I played through half of P5 then I stopped around the time you get to the desert palace. I’ve attempted to revisit it several times but I soldiered on this time. This time I was determined to finish it. [b]I’m glad I did.[/b] This game is just absolute style. It oozes cool. Atlus really cooked with this. So i’ll just lay out my thoughts: [h3]The Good: [/h3] What this game does right is slick art direction. A compelling enough story about rebellion tackling themes of identity and self. Art direction is exquisite. I’ve seen people say this game makes them feel like superheroes and I kind of get that. The turn based combat is light (even on harder difficulties the game is a breeze) The social systems are pretty interesting. Characters are developed (including the side characters) and are memorable, bopping music, gorgeous art. This game really is an anime. [h3]The Bad: [/h3] This game really is an anime. If you dislike anime, you’re going to dislike some aspects of this game. I don't want to get too much into spoilers, but sometimes characters are easy to predict, archetypes of characters are also very obvious. Settings like beach episodes and firework festivals happen… Also you’ve got some fan service-y moments that can be hit or miss. All of that build leads to [spoiler]fighting god [/spoiler]. I was enjoying the rebelling against the system story until [spoiler] the holy grail starts sucking off everyone’s free will and it turns out the big bad was the velvet room guy… who turns out to be the demonic manifestation of choice and isn’t the real velvet room guy…. And he split the attendant into two small annoying little girls who abuse you [/spoiler] This game is really easy. Sometimes it boils down to outdamaging your opponent. And if you play smart a number of encounters are trivial…. Except for the [spoiler]Okumura boss fight… That fight was ass[/spoiler] [h2]Conclusion: Go get it, its retardedly good[/h2] I don't think you can sing this game’s praises enough. Each accolade earned. I will say for an older game it's a bit on the steep side so wait for a sale, but I'd absolutely recommend you play this. Great bang for your buck and if you missed things, its NG+ adds a ton.

this is the first time i played a game that made me feel nostalgic for a life i never actually lived and grieve a youth i never had. persona 5 royal is obviously an incredible game from top to bottom. the soundtrack, the art direction, the characters, the story, all of it. but what really stuck with me wasn't the palaces or fighting corrupt adults. it was the little things. walking home after school, studying at leblanc while it rains outside, making plans with friends, having people who genuinely want you around. there's something so bittersweet about spending hundreds of hours with a group of fictional characters who slowly start to feel like your own friends. especially when your actual teenage years looked nothing like that. i think that's what makes persona so special, but also so painful. it gives you this beautiful version of youth where every day feels like an opportunity, where friendships grow if you put in the effort, where even the most ordinary afternoons can turn into memories worth keeping. and then it reminds you that time is limited. you can't do everything, you can't be everywhere, and eventually, you have to say goodbye. it was pretty strange to finish the game and find myself mourning not just the characters but all the experiences i never got to have. the friendships i never made, the invitations i turned down, the person i might've been if things had gone a little differently. but i guess that's also the point. you can't go back and redo your teenage years, and real life doesn't have a calendar telling you exactly how many days you have left with someone. all you can really do is make the most of the time you still have. i started this game thinking it looked cool. i finished it wishing i'd lived a little more, and wanting to make sure i don't keep making that same mistake. 10/10. came for the phantom thieves, left with an existential crisis and a newfound appreciation for being alive. take your time.

I just completed my first playthrough and this game is another masterpiece. At this point I am an atlus fanboy, so maybe the masterpiece thing was a bit biased (but I don't feel like it). When I'm writing this review, I already finished the game and doing my 2nd run on NG+. Persona 5 Royal is the game that made persona franchise known to a lot of people and I can see why. Most of the people who are new to JRPGs and experienced persona in the modern day (PS4 - PS5 era) they start with P5R. It definitely a game with easier combat than traditional JRPGs or the predecessor of the game (P4G). I would say the combat mechanics are cool and it's a good thing that they introduced to the game, but somehow it made combat feels easier. However, I found that some people just cannot tolerate the old JRPGs combat like on P4G to play, or even the graphics (since this game is released on a more modern era). They not even touch the older games and still say that this is the best game ever, talking about a spoiled, pampered gamer, I can't stand this kind of new persona fan. Back to the game aspects, I feel like some of the character are poorly written at some point, like Morgana in the beginning to the middle part of the game who always trash-talking Ryuji for no reason, Ann that sexualized a lot. The grinding aspects also bored me since it's basically Tartarus with less floors and it went downwards. But, this is truly the most epic, stylish persona games. The after school and evening session is also a great improvements with the players are being able to walk throughout Tokyo with the Third Person camera, giving a sensation of what daily life feels like in Tokyo. What I would recommend to new players getting into Persona franchise, just start with whatever your heart feels or real world situation you currently facing. For example, P5R is about rebellion to the corrupt system, P4G is about accepting your true self and warm friendship, P3 is about live your best life in the moment because we don't know what tomorrow will bring. I had a good time playing this game, even though P4G is still another level of Persona games. And if you wanna play this game, just prepared for a long journey because this is the longest persona games. P.S: I used to think Kasumi is the best girl but after I finished the game, it definitely is Makoto and Futaba. If you feel like you wanna get as much experience for the first playthrough just romance everyone. Temperance and Fortune confidants are the most beneficial. This game is incredible. An addicting JRPG where you balance fighting in the metaverse being the hero the people need whilst living an honest, student's life. Before I knew it, 100 hours had flown by and I was saying goodbye to the amazing friends I made along the way.. Pros: Music - The songs in this game are BANGERS. They perfectly match the theme of what you're meant to feel and never get boring regardless of how many times you hear them. Story - There's always another boss to take down. There's always someone bigger, BADDER, more threatening. The main storyline mixed with the side dramas of NPCs is well written and engaging. Companions - I cared about every single companion I had. They're all detailed and undergo a story arc that compels you to learn more about them and appreciate the time you spend together. They're all unique and detestable at first but once you get to know them they feel like family. Freedom of Choice - This game is heavily time based and how you choose to spend your time keeps you engaged but also allows you to play the game you want. There is no right way to play and the people you choose to spend your time with or the activities that you do are purely up to you. If you want to spend every night at the bath house with old men that's chill. Voice Acting - Every character's voice actor did a phenomenal job. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Mixed: Combat - Combat is fun but feels repetitive after a while. It's basically a Pokemon style battle system where you utilize enemy weaknesses to create an advantage with some items to use mixed in. Personas - Persona crafting is fun but it got to a point where I had my main set of 8 Personas or so and stopped fusing from there. There's a lot of depth in Persona fusion, creation, strengthening that I didn't explore but it seemed alright for the most part. Itemization / Chests / Loot - Was interesting at first but you quickly realize that you can just go to one shop and purchase all of the best possible items as long as you have the funds. Opening chests never felt amazing like it does in other games but wasn't negative either. Romance - The romance is there if you try for it but never goes too deep. I'm one to try to date/romance as many characters as possible but because I cared so much for these characters I only romanced one. Main Character - It's undeniable that the main character has an insane amount of aura but when he talks he never really says much. It's almost like you're an NPC living in a world with your companions with how much personality and charm THEY have. At the end of the day, you're the main character but the dialogue options are very minimal and he rarely ever speaks (voice acting wise). -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Cons: Interrogating Personas - I have over 100 hours in this game and I still couldn't crack the code on what personas want to hear during interrogations. Your companions might mention what they WANT to hear but half the time it seems like it still doesn't correlate to what they need to hear to be successful. Limited Dialogue Options - This might not be a big deal to most people but after a while I began to notice I was playing the game only to tell companions what they wanted to hear to boost up our relationship. I turned into a "Yes Man" in order to maximize my stats because time is precious and I couldn't spend it saying the words I wanted to if it wasn't going to give me any benefit outside of a chuckle. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Overall this game is an absolute masterpiece and will change the lives of the people who play it.
